title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Four distinct questions, each with its own clinical trigger.

Is there intraperitoneal free fluid? In trauma, free fluid = blood until proven otherwise. In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent ascites, hollow viscus perforation, or internal hemorrhage.
Is there a distended, obstructed bladder? Urinary retention is a common, painful, and easily treated problem — one that is frequently missed in sedated or altered patients.
Is there hydronephrosis? Ureteral obstruction causing hydronephrosis may explain AKI, flank pain, or urosepsis in an undrained system.
In the trauma patient — is there free fluid in the pericardium? The subxiphoid FAST view incorporates cardiac assessment (see Module 1).



Abdominal ultrasound at the bedside is fast, non-invasive, and immediately actionable. The FAST exam (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is the standard of care in trauma resuscitation. In non-trauma critical care, bladder and kidney assessment are high-yield applications that require minimal additional training.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a curvilinear (low-frequency, 2–5 MHz) probe for all abdominal windows — the penetration depth required for the liver, spleen, kidneys, and pelvis exceeds what a linear probe provides. A phased array probe is an acceptable substitute for FAST but is less ideal for the pelvic view.
Machine preset: Abdominal. Adjust depth to see structures of interest with adequate margin.


Right upper quadrant — Morrison’s pouch






Tip



Video slot: RUQ acquisition — hepatorenal interface, fan through Morrison’s pouch, assess for free fluid.


Probe placement: Probe in the right mid-axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the patient’s head. Fan through the hepatorenal interface (Morrison’s pouch) — the potential space between the liver and right kidney.
What you are looking for: Any anechoic (black) stripe between the liver and right kidney. In a normal exam, the liver and kidney appear to be in direct contact with a thin hyperechoic stripe of Gerota’s fascia between them. Free fluid appears as a wedge or stripe of anechoic material in the dependent hepatorenal space. Also assess the inferior tip of the liver and the right paracolic gutter.
Pearls: Morrison’s pouch is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine position and the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible here.



Left upper quadrant — splenorenal space






Tip



Video slot: LUQ acquisition — splenorenal interface, subphrenic space, left paracolic gutter.


Probe placement: Left posterior axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the head. This window is more posterior than the RUQ view — a common error is imaging too anteriorly and missing the spleen.
What you are looking for: Free fluid between the spleen and left kidney (splenorenal space), and in the subphrenic space (between the diaphragm and spleen). A left pleural effusion appears above the diaphragm — do not confuse it with subphrenic free fluid. The diaphragm is the landmark: fluid above = pleural, fluid below = peritoneal.
Pearls: The LUQ is less sensitive than the RUQ because the splenorenal space is less dependent. Free fluid may not accumulate here until larger volumes are present. Assess the subphrenic and paracolic regions thoroughly.



Suprapubic — pelvis






Tip



Video slot: Suprapubic acquisition — bladder as acoustic window, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (female) or rectovesical space (male), transverse and sagittal planes.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, just above the symphysis pubis, indicator to the patient’s right (transverse) or head (sagittal). The bladder serves as an acoustic window to the posterior pelvic structures.
What you are looking for: Free fluid posterior to the bladder (pouch of Douglas in females, rectovesical space in males). In females, look for fluid in the cul-de-sac posterior to the uterus. Scan in both transverse and sagittal planes. Free fluid appears anechoic, dependent, and irregular in shape.
Bladder assessment: See dedicated section below.
Pearls: The pelvic view requires a full or at least partially full bladder to serve as an acoustic window. In patients who are oliguric or have been catheterized, the pelvic view may be limited. The pelvic space is the most dependent location in the erect position — significant fluid may accumulate here even when the upper quadrants appear negative.



Subxiphoid — pericardium and cardiac
Covered in Module 1. The subxiphoid view is the fourth standard FAST window.



Bladder — transverse and sagittal






Tip



Video slot: Bladder assessment — full bladder as an anechoic structure, volume estimation, wall assessment.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, transverse then sagittal. The bladder appears as a well-defined anechoic structure posterior to the symphysis. Measure three dimensions: transverse (width), anteroposterior (depth), and craniocaudal (height). Bladder volume (mL) ≈ 0.52 × width × depth × height (in cm). Some machines calculate this automatically.
Significant residual volume: >300 mL post-void, or a distended bladder in a patient with reduced consciousness who is not catheterized.



Kidneys — longitudinal






Tip



Video slot: Right and left kidney — normal cortex and collecting system vs hydronephrosis grades.


Probe placement: Coronal plane, similar to FAST views but oriented to the kidneys. Right kidney: right mid-axillary line, indicator up. Left kidney: left posterior axillary line, indicator up. Obtain a longitudinal image of the entire kidney — cortex, medullary pyramids, and collecting system (renal pelvis and calyces).
What you are looking for: Any separation of the renal sinus (echogenic central collecting system) by anechoic fluid — indicating hydronephrosis.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal FAST exam — no free fluid at each window. Normal kidney. Normal bladder.



Normal FAST exam
No anechoic fluid in Morrison’s pouch, splenorenal space, or pelvis. The subxiphoid view shows no pericardial effusion. Organ surfaces are in direct contact with each other and with the abdominal wall.


Normal kidney
Length 9–12 cm, width 4–6 cm. The renal cortex is slightly less echogenic than the liver. The renal sinus (collecting system) appears as a central echogenic structure without internal fluid. Medullary pyramids appear as hypoechoic triangular structures pointing toward the sinus.


Normal bladder
Thin-walled, smooth, anechoic. Wall thickness <3 mm when full. Urine is anechoic; debris, clots, or calculi appear as echogenic foci within the lumen.


Perihepatic fat and ascites mimics
Small amounts of fat around the liver and mesentery can mimic minimal free fluid. Fat has a characteristic echogenicity (not purely anechoic) and does not layer into dependent spaces the way free fluid does. Bowel loops with fluid should not be mistaken for free fluid — identify peristalsis and bowel wall to distinguish.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding.

Free fluid — traumatic (hemoperitoneum)






Tip



Video slots: - Anechoic free fluid in Morrison’s pouch - Moderate-large free fluid in the pelvis - Echogenic free fluid — acute blood


In trauma, any free fluid is assumed to be blood. Acute hemoperitoneum may be anechoic (early, not clotted) or echogenic (clotted blood). The pattern and volume guide management.
Grading by volume and distribution:








Finding
Estimated Volume
Management Implication




Trace fluid in Morrison’s pouch only
<250 mL
Serial exam, reassess


Fluid in RUQ + pelvis
500–1000 mL
Operative vs non-operative decision based on hemodynamics


Fluid in all three windows
>1000 mL
Likely operative in hemodynamically unstable patient



Teaching points:

A positive FAST in a hemodynamically unstable patient = OR, not CT. Do not delay operative intervention for imaging.
A negative FAST does not rule out intraperitoneal injury — solid organ injuries may be present without free fluid early.
A positive FAST in a hemodynamically stable patient allows CT for better injury characterization before operative decision.
Echogenic (bright) free fluid = acute blood/clot. Anechoic free fluid in trauma = blood (until proven otherwise), even if it looks like simple fluid.




Free fluid — non-traumatic






Tip



Video slot: Ascites — large volume anechoic free fluid surrounding bowel loops, “floating” bowel.


In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent: - Ascites: Cirrhosis, malignancy, heart failure — anechoic, often massive, bowel loops appear to float - Ruptured viscus: Bowel perforation — complex, echogenic, or mixed fluid - Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: Pelvic free fluid in a woman of childbearing age = ectopic until proven otherwise - Internal hemorrhage: Post-procedural, anticoagulated, aortic aneurysm rupture
Teaching points:

In a non-trauma patient with hypotension and pelvic free fluid, always check a urine or serum beta-hCG before attributing fluid to another cause.
Ruptured ectopic with free fluid and hemodynamic instability = emergent gynecologic surgery.
Large ascites can be drained under ultrasound guidance (see Module 11).




Urinary retention and bladder assessment






Tip



Video slots: - Massively distended bladder — large anechoic structure filling the pelvis - Bladder volume calculation with three-plane measurement


A distended bladder (>300 mL post-void residual) in a patient with reduced consciousness, confusion, agitation, or unexplained pain is urinary retention until proven otherwise.
Teaching points:

Urinary retention is common in the ICU — opioids, anticholinergics, and sedatives all reduce detrusor function.
In a male patient with an enlarged prostate, any acute illness may precipitate retention.
A fully distended bladder (>500–800 mL) can reflexively inhibit cardiac output and worsen hemodynamics.
Treatment is urethral or suprapubic catheterization. Ultrasound-guided suprapubic catheterization is appropriate when urethral access is not possible.
Post-decompression diuresis can occur after relief of chronic obstruction — anticipate and replace fluids.




Hydronephrosis






Tip



Video slots: - Grade 1 hydronephrosis — mild dilation of the renal pelvis only - Grade 2 — dilation of pelvis and calyces, preserved cortex - Grade 3 — severe dilation, thinned cortex


Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal collecting system from ureteral obstruction. It appears as anechoic fluid within the renal sinus, separating the echogenic collecting system walls.
Grading:



Grade
Appearance




1 (mild)
Pelvis dilated, calyces normal


2 (moderate)
Pelvis and calyces dilated, cortex preserved


3 (severe)
Marked dilation, cortex thinned



Teaching points:

Hydronephrosis in a patient with AKI = obstructive nephropathy until proven otherwise. Relieve the obstruction (Foley, ureteral stent, nephrostomy) before attributing the AKI to another cause.
Bilateral hydronephrosis = bilateral obstruction or bladder outlet obstruction (BPH, mass). Check the bladder first.
Hydronephrosis + fever = obstructed, infected system (pyonephrosis) — urgent drainage is required (not just antibiotics).
Normal ultrasound does not rule out obstruction in early or acute cases — the collecting system may not have had time to dilate.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Trauma — positive FAST in a hypotensive patient
Clinical scenario: A 25-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision at highway speed. He is hypotensive (BP 78/50) and tachycardic (HR 132) on arrival. GCS is 14. The trauma team is assembled.
What exam would you perform? Immediate FAST exam as part of the primary survey.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Morrison’s pouch: free fluid, moderate volume. Splenorenal space: free fluid. Pelvis: large volume free fluid. Subxiphoid: no pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Positive FAST with hemodynamic instability = operative intervention. Do not take this patient to CT. Transfuse blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC:FFP:platelets) as a bridge to the OR. Activate massive transfusion protocol. The trauma surgeon takes over — the bedside echo has already answered the most important question.



Case 2: Urosepsis with flank pain — is the system obstructed?
Clinical scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of kidney stones presents with fever (39.2°C), right flank pain, and hypotension. UA shows pyuria. He is started on IV antibiotics and fluids. The team is wondering if he needs urgent urologic intervention.
What exam would you perform? Renal ultrasound — bilateral kidneys.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Right kidney: grade 2–3 hydronephrosis. Echogenic material within the dilated collecting system (debris). Left kidney: normal.
How does this change management? Obstructed, infected right kidney — pyonephrosis. Antibiotics alone are insufficient. Emergent urology consultation for urgent drainage — either ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Septic shock from an obstructed system will not resolve without drainage. This is a surgical emergency, not a medical one.



Case 3: Altered mental status and agitation — is this retention?
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with BPH, on post-op day 1 following a hip replacement, is increasingly agitated and confused. Vitals are stable. He received significant opioids intraoperatively. His Foley was removed 4 hours ago.
What exam would you perform? Bladder ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Distended, smooth-walled bladder. Estimated volume 680 mL.
How does this change management? Urinary retention causing agitation and delirium in a post-operative elderly male. Replace the urethral catheter. Agitation should resolve within minutes of bladder decompression. Avoid sedatives — they will worsen delirium without treating the cause. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis. Address BPH pharmacologically (alpha-blocker) before the next void trial.



Case 4: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ED with sudden-onset lower abdominal pain and presyncope. BP 90/60, HR 118. She reports her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She thought she might be pregnant but has not confirmed it.
What exam would you perform? FAST exam with attention to the pelvic view, and immediate beta-hCG.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Large volume of free fluid in the pelvis and RUQ. No intrauterine pregnancy visible. Echogenic mass adjacent to the left ovary. Beta-hCG returns at 4,200 mIU/mL.
How does this change management? Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum. This is a surgical emergency. Call OB/GYN for emergent surgical intervention. Two large-bore IVs, blood type and crossmatch, activate the OR. Do not perform a diagnostic laparoscopy — this patient needs a therapeutic laparotomy or laparoscopy. Time is critical.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. Where is the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid in a supine patient, and why?






Caution





Answer Morrison’s pouch (the hepatorenal space in the right upper quadrant) is the most sensitive location because it is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine patient. Fluid accumulates there preferentially due to gravity. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible at this location before it is detectable elsewhere.



Q2. A FAST exam is negative in a hemodynamically stable trauma patient with abdominal tenderness. What is the next step?






Caution





Answer A negative FAST does not rule out solid organ injury or retroperitoneal injury. In a stable patient with abdominal tenderness and a mechanism concerning for injury, CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the next step. CT has much higher sensitivity than ultrasound for detecting solid organ lacerations that have not yet bled into the peritoneum.



Q3. You detect hydronephrosis in a patient with new AKI. What is the next clinical question?






Caution





Answer Is the obstruction bilateral or unilateral? Bilateral hydronephrosis (or hydronephrosis in a solitary kidney) explains AKI — the obstruction must be relieved urgently. Unilateral hydronephrosis alone does not explain AKI unless the contralateral kidney is absent or non-functional. Also ask: is there fever or signs of infection? If so, the obstructed system is infected (pyonephrosis) and requires emergent drainage, not just observation.



Q4. A left pleural effusion appears as fluid above the diaphragm on the LUQ view. How do you distinguish it from subphrenic free fluid?






Caution





Answer The diaphragm is the key landmark — it appears as a bright echogenic curved line. Pleural fluid is above the diaphragm (between the lung and the diaphragm). Peritoneal free fluid is below the diaphragm (in the subphrenic or splenorenal space). The “mirror artifact” — a mirror image of the spleen or liver appearing above the diaphragm — is a normal artifact in the absence of pleural fluid. The presence of a true anechoic collection above the diaphragm that does not show the mirror artifact indicates a pleural effusion.



Q5. Why is pelvic free fluid in a woman of reproductive age a critical finding that requires immediate additional testing?






Caution





Answer Pelvic free fluid in a reproductive-age woman must be evaluated for ruptured ectopic pregnancy — a life-threatening condition that can produce rapid exsanguination. A urine or serum beta-hCG must be obtained immediately. If beta-hCG is positive and there is no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound, ruptured ectopic is highly likely until proven otherwise. Hemodynamic instability with pelvic free fluid and a positive beta-hCG = emergent surgical intervention, not further imaging.

section: 2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
text:
2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
A systematic framework for the undifferentiated hemodynamically unstable patient.
Every bedside echo in shock should answer these four questions, in this order:
1. Is there a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology? If yes, stop — this is the diagnosis and the intervention is pericardiocentesis. Do not proceed with a hemodynamic workup until tamponade is excluded or treated.
2. What is LV systolic function? Severely reduced = cardiogenic component. Hyperdynamic = distributive or hypovolemic. Normal requires further assessment.
3. What is RV size and function? Dilated RV with D-sign and a normal or hyperdynamic LV = obstructive physiology (PE) or acute cor pulmonale until proven otherwise. RV dilation with reduced LV function = biventricular failure.
4. What is the IVC? Small and collapsible = low filling pressure, possible fluid responsiveness. Large and non-collapsing = elevated filling pressure, fluid loading is unlikely to help.






Tip



Video slot: Demonstration of a systematic 4-question exam — subcostal (pericardium + IVC), PLAX (LV + pericardium), PSAX (D-sign, LV function), apical 4-chamber (RV:LV ratio, LV wall motion).

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
4. When findings conflict
The exam doesn’t always give you a clean answer.






Tip



Video slot: Mixed shock state — reduced EF with small IVC; how to interpret and what to do.


Common conflicting scenarios and how to reason through them:
Reduced EF + small IVC The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — the patient is hypovolemic relative to their baseline. A cautious fluid trial (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output without tipping into pulmonary edema. Monitor closely.
Hyperdynamic LV + plethoric IVC High-output state with elevated venous pressure. Consider: severe sepsis with right heart congestion, severe tricuspid regurgitation, hepatic disease, or a patient in compensated high-output heart failure who has been aggressively fluid-loaded.
Normal LV + dilated RV + plethoric IVC (no effusion) Obstructive physiology from PE or acute cor pulmonale from ARDS. Do not give more fluid. Focus on diagnosis and afterload reduction.
Large effusion + no tamponade physiology + plethoric IVC Consider chronic effusion (malignant, uremic) with concomitant right heart failure causing the elevated IVC — these are two separate problems. Treat both.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
5. Serial exams and trending
Echo is not a one-time test.






Tip



Video slot: Before/after comparison — echo before and after 1 L fluid bolus in a patient with septic shock.


The true power of bedside echo in critical care is the ability to perform serial exams and track the response to interventions in real time. Key scenarios for repeat assessment:

After a fluid bolus: Did IVC diameter change? Did cardiac output improve (visual or measured)? Did venous congestion worsen?
After vasopressor dose change: Did LV or RV filling improve?
After diuresis: Is venous congestion resolving? Is IVC size decreasing?
After pericardiocentesis: Is tamponade physiology resolved? Is there residual constrictive physiology?
Trending over hours: Is RV function improving with treatment of PE or ARDS? Is EF recovering in myocarditis?

Each exam should be compared to the prior exam, not interpreted in isolation. Document the key findings (EF category, RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter, IVC collapsibility) so that trends are visible across shifts.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
6. Integration cases
Complex cases requiring synthesis of all modules.


Case 1: The patient in undifferentiated shock
Clinical scenario: A 64-year-old man with no significant cardiac history is transferred from a community hospital with “septic shock, possible PE.” He has been on norepinephrine for 6 hours and received 5 L of crystalloid. On arrival: BP 74/48, HR 128, temp 37.8°C, O2 sat 90% on 6 L NC. He is slightly confused. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Troponin is mildly elevated.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — complete four-window exam.


What you see: 1. No pericardial effusion. 2. LV severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis, no RWMA. 3. RV moderately dilated. D-sign present. McConnell’s sign absent. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC 2.5 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: This is not simple septic shock. The severely reduced LV EF with RV dilation and a plethoric IVC suggests biventricular failure. The bilateral infiltrates could reflect pulmonary edema rather than pneumonia. The elevated troponin is consistent with cardiogenic shock. The differential includes new dilated cardiomyopathy with acute decompensation, fulminant myocarditis, or sepsis-induced biventricular dysfunction.
How does this change management? Stop fluids — the patient is congested. Add dobutamine for inotropic support. Get a 12-lead ECG and urgent formal echo. Consider PA catheter to characterize hemodynamics. The “sepsis” label may be wrong — treat aggressively for a primary cardiac event. If troponin is significantly elevated and ECG shows ischemic changes, activate the cath lab.



Case 2: Post-arrest resuscitation — what caused the arrest?
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman had a witnessed cardiac arrest in the hospital corridor. She was resuscitated in 8 minutes with 2 shocks and CPR. Now intubated, hemodynamically marginal on vasopressors. No prior cardiac history. The team wants to know: VF arrest from ACS, PE, or something else?
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.



What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: anterior and apical wall akinesis. Severely reduced EF. No global hypokinesis — the inferior and lateral walls move. 3. RV: normal size. No D-sign. Normal TAPSE. 4. IVC: 2.0 cm, 30% collapse (borderline).
Integration: Regional wall motion abnormality in the anterior/LAD distribution with a normal RV. This is a large anterior STEMI causing VF arrest. The RV is not dilated — this is not a PE causing the arrest. The IVC is borderline, consistent with post-resuscitation state.
How does this change management? Activate the cath lab immediately for emergent PCI. This is STEMI-equivalent post-arrest — coronary angiography is indicated regardless of the post-resuscitation ECG. Initiate targeted temperature management per protocol. The echo finding of an anterior RWMA pointing to the LAD is the critical finding that directs the team to the right intervention.



Case 3: Hypoxic respiratory failure — cardiac or pulmonary?
Clinical scenario: A 71-year-old woman with COPD is admitted with progressive dyspnea over 3 days. She is hypoxic (O2 sat 84% on 10 L), hypotensive (BP 90/60), and has bilateral crackles and lower extremity edema. BNP is 1,800 pg/mL. Chest X-ray shows bilateral opacities. The team is debating whether to intubate for COPD exacerbation or initiate diuresis for decompensated heart failure.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: severely reduced EF, dilated — chronic appearance. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign (diastolic flattening, consistent with volume overload). 4. IVC: 2.8 cm, non-collapsing. Hepatic veins dilated.
Integration: Decompensated heart failure with reduced EF, biventricular volume overload, and severe congestion — not a primary COPD exacerbation. The COPD may be contributing to increased RV afterload, but the dominant pathophysiology is cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
How does this change management? Initiate NIV (BiPAP) to reduce preload and work of breathing. Begin aggressive diuresis. Add dobutamine if hemodynamics do not improve with afterload and preload reduction. Do not intubate for COPD management — the indication, if intubation becomes necessary, is respiratory failure from cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Treat the heart.



Case 4: The patient who “isn’t responding” to treatment
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with known COPD and newly diagnosed lung cancer was admitted 3 days ago for presumed COPD exacerbation. He has been on bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics with minimal improvement. He remains hypoxic and increasingly vasopressor-dependent. Repeat echo is requested by the ICU attending.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. Moderate pericardial effusion. No RA or RV collapse. IVC plethoric. 2. LV: normal EF. No RWMA. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign present (pressure overload pattern — systolic flattening). 4. IVC: 2.4 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: Two separate findings: a pericardial effusion (likely malignant) and RV pressure overload without tamponade physiology. The effusion is not causing tamponade. The RV dilation with pressure-overload D-sign in a patient with lung cancer raises the possibility of pulmonary hypertension from tumor invasion, PE, or extrinsic pulmonary vascular compression. Neither finding fits a primary COPD exacerbation.
How does this change management? CT pulmonary angiography to evaluate for PE and pulmonary vascular involvement by tumor. Oncology consultation for the effusion (malignant pericardial effusion likely). Reframe the clinical diagnosis — this is not a COPD exacerbation. The failure to respond to bronchodilators and steroids was a clue that the diagnosis was wrong.



Case 5: The post-operative patient who won’t come off the ventilator
Clinical scenario: A 69-year-old man undergoes elective aortic valve replacement. He is extubated on post-op day 2 but reintubated 6 hours later for respiratory failure. He is now post-op day 5, sedated, and failing repeated extubation trials. An ICU team requests bedside echo to evaluate hemodynamics.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — post-surgical windows (often challenging).


What you see: 1. Small anterior effusion. No chamber collapse. 2. LV: EF 45% (mildly reduced, new compared to pre-op 60%). Anterior wall motion mildly reduced. 3. RV: mildly dilated. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC: 2.2 cm, 20% distensibility (borderline for fluid responsiveness in a ventilated patient).
Integration: New mild LV dysfunction (post-operative stunned myocardium vs perioperative MI), mild RV dysfunction, and borderline volume status. The anterior wall motion abnormality raises concern for a perioperative LAD event. The ventricular dysfunction is driving respiratory failure — the patient is not failing extubation from pulmonary mechanics but from hemodynamic compromise.
How does this change management? Obtain an ECG and serial troponins — a perioperative MI must be ruled out. Cardiology consultation for post-surgical echo. Optimize hemodynamics: gentle diuresis to reduce preload, optimize heart rate, consider low-dose inotrope if EF remains depressed. Address the cardiac problem before the next extubation trial — the respiratory failure is a symptom, not the diagnosis.






Tip



Integration reminder: The power of the four-question exam is not in any single finding. It is in the composite picture and the management decision that follows.

Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. A patient in shock has a hyperdynamic LV, a dilated RV with D-sign, and a plethoric IVC. No pericardial effusion. What is the most likely hemodynamic phenotype and the priority intervention?






Caution





Answer Obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism (or acute cor pulmonale). The hyperdynamic LV is underfilled due to RV failure impairing output. The priority is reducing RV afterload — systemic anticoagulation, and in hemodynamic collapse, systemic thrombolytics or catheter-directed therapy. Do not give fluid boluses.



Q2. You find a severely reduced EF and a small, collapsible IVC in a hypotensive patient. What does this suggest and how do you manage it?






Caution





Answer The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — cardiogenic shock superimposed on hypovolemia (or volume depletion from prior diuresis/bleeding). A cautious fluid challenge (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output. Monitor closely for pulmonary edema. Add inotropic support if the EF does not improve with preload optimization.



Q3. After performing a bedside echo, you are unsure whether the reduced EF is new or chronic. How does the LV size help you distinguish?






Caution





Answer A dilated LV suggests a chronic process — the heart has had time to remodel. A non-dilated LV with severely reduced EF suggests an acute process (myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute MI, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy). Acuity changes the differential and the urgency of investigation (e.g., emergent cath lab for suspected acute MI vs. supportive management for myocarditis).



Q4. A patient’s echo shows: no effusion, normal LV, dilated RV with McConnell’s sign, plethoric IVC. What is the diagnosis and what is the single most important intervention?






Caution





Answer Massive pulmonary embolism with RV failure. The single most important intervention is systemic thrombolysis (if no contraindication) — it rapidly reduces RV afterload by dissolving the clot. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient in hemodynamic collapse. Activate a PE response team or get interventional radiology and cardiac surgery on the line simultaneously.



Q5. What is the purpose of serial bedside echo in the ICU, and what should be documented to make serial exams useful?






Caution





Answer Serial echo tracks the response to interventions and identifies deterioration or recovery over time. A single exam is a snapshot; serial exams reveal trajectory. Document key quantitative or semi-quantitative findings at each exam: EF category (severely reduced / mildly reduced / normal / hyperdynamic), RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter and collapsibility, presence of chamber collapse or D-sign. This allows any clinician picking up the patient to immediately understand where the hemodynamics started and where they are now.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Three questions in order.

Is there a pericardial effusion? An echo-free space surrounding the heart — confirmed in at least two views before acting on it.
Is it physiologically significant? Size alone does not determine significance. Look for chamber collapse, plethoric IVC, and respiratory variation — the hallmarks of elevated intrapericardial pressure.
Does this change what you do right now? Tamponade is a clinical and sonographic diagnosis. A large effusion in a hemodynamically stable patient may warrant monitoring and urgent cardiology consultation. The same effusion in a hypotensive patient with RA collapse is a needle emergency.

Two further questions apply in the non-acute setting:

Is this pericarditis, and does it require intervention? Echo defines the effusion, tracks its size, and identifies patients at highest risk.
Is this constrictive pericarditis? Constriction is the great mimic of right heart failure and the one pericardial diagnosis that requires surgical intervention.



Pericardial ultrasound answers a binary, time-sensitive question at the bedside: does this patient need pericardiocentesis now? It also identifies effusions that will influence resuscitation strategy — for example, recognizing that aggressive fluid loading in tamponade provides only a brief bridge, and that vasopressors are a temporizing measure, not a solution. In the subacute setting, recognizing pericarditis and constriction prevents missed diagnoses that carry significant long-term consequences.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. The four standard windows are covered in Module 1. For pericardial assessment, the subcostal view is obtained first in an unstable patient; PLAX and apical four-chamber provide complementary information. This module adds Doppler assessment for constrictive physiology.
Depth: Ensure the posterior pericardium is fully visible with a small margin beyond it. A common error is insufficient depth that clips the posterior effusion.


Subcostal four-chamber — pericardial assessment






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal view for pericardial assessment — effusion, RA free wall collapse, RV diastolic collapse.


The RV free wall is nearest the probe, making the subcostal view the best window for detecting RA and RV chamber collapse in tamponade. The entire pericardium can be surveyed by fanning through the cardiac silhouette.



Parasternal long axis — pericardial assessment






Tip



Video slot: PLAX for pericardial assessment — posterior effusion, descending aorta landmark, effusion sizing.



Effusion on PLAX appears as an echo-free stripe posterior to the LV. Key landmark: the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section at the far left of the image. Fluid anterior to the aorta is pericardial; fluid posterior to the aorta is pleural.



Apical four-chamber — pericardial assessment






Tip



Video slot: Apical four-chamber for pericardial assessment — circumferential effusion, RA collapse, respiratory variation on mitral inflow.


The apical view is useful for identifying loculated effusions and for PW Doppler assessment of respiratory variation across the mitral valve in suspected tamponade.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal pericardium in each window. Normal mitral inflow Doppler. Normal hepatic vein flow.




Normal pericardium
A thin, bright (hyperechoic) line surrounding the heart that moves with it. No echo-free space between the visceral and parietal layers. A physiologic trace of fluid (up to 50 mL) may appear as a very thin stripe posteriorly on PLAX — this does not warrant intervention.


Pericardial fat pad
The most common mimic of pericardial effusion. Pericardial fat is echogenic (bright, not black), most prominent anteriorly, and does not shift with patient repositioning. Key distinguishing features:

Fat is echogenic; effusion is anechoic.
Fat does not change with the cardiac cycle; effusion may show swirling.
Fat is anterior; hemodynamically significant effusions tend to be circumferential and posterior.



Epicardial fat
Sits between the myocardium and the visceral pericardium. Visible as a thin echogenic layer over the RV free wall and in the AV groove. Moves with the heart (unlike pericardial fat pad, which is relatively fixed). Differentiated from a small effusion by echogenicity and motion pattern.


Post-CABG appearance
After cardiac surgery, the pericardium is often left open or partially closed, creating atypical appearances with adhesions and thickening. Post-operative effusions are frequently anterior and loculated. Subcostal view may be normal — always check all windows in post-surgical patients with new hemodynamic instability.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Small effusion






Tip



Video slot: Small posterior effusion on PLAX — thin echo-free stripe, preserved chamber function.


Less than 1 cm in greatest diameter on PLAX, posterior to the LV. Visible in diastole; may thin or disappear in systole.
Teaching points:

Accumulates posteriorly first — the most dependent space in the supine patient.
Does not produce chamber collapse.
Causes: pericarditis, viral illness, malignancy, uremia, post-procedure.
In the right clinical context (pleuritic chest pain, friction rub), a small effusion supports acute pericarditis and warrants NSAIDs and follow-up imaging — not drainage.




Moderate to large effusion






Tip



Video slot: Large circumferential effusion — swinging heart, echo-free space in all windows.




Moderate: 1–2 cm; large: >2 cm on PLAX. Large effusions are typically circumferential and visible in all windows.
Teaching points:

The “swinging heart” — pendular cardiac motion within the effusion — is a marker of significant hemodynamic risk.
Size does not equal tamponade. A large chronic effusion (e.g., malignant) may be tolerated because the pericardium has had time to stretch. An acute effusion of even 200 mL (e.g., post-procedure, trauma) can cause tamponade because the pericardium has not had time to accommodate.
Always assess chamber collapse and IVC when a large effusion is present.




Tamponade physiology






Tip



Video slots: - RA free wall collapse in systole (subcostal or apical) - RV diastolic collapse (PLAX or subcostal) - Plethoric, non-collapsing IVC - Respiratory variation on mitral inflow (M-mode or PW Doppler)




Tamponade is elevated intrapericardial pressure exceeding intracardiac filling pressure. It is a clinical diagnosis confirmed sonographically. No single finding is pathognomonic — the diagnosis is integrative.
Sonographic findings, in order of sensitivity:








Finding
View
Notes




RA free wall collapse (systole)
Subcostal, apical
Earliest sign; sensitive but not specific


RV diastolic collapse
PLAX, subcostal
More specific; correlates with pressure equalization


Plethoric IVC (>2.1 cm, <50% collapse)
Subcostal IVC view
Reflects elevated right-sided filling pressures


Respiratory variation on mitral inflow >25%
Apical, PW Doppler
Sonographic equivalent of pulsus paradoxus



Management implication: When tamponade physiology is present in a hemodynamically unstable patient, the exam is over. Call for pericardiocentesis or emergent cardiothoracic surgery depending on the clinical context. Do not delay for formal echo.



Loculated effusion






Tip



Video slot: Post-operative loculated effusion — anterior, irregular, compressing a single chamber.




Loculated effusions do not distribute freely. They occur after cardiac surgery, trauma, or prior pericarditis with adhesions. The collection may compress only one chamber, producing atypical hemodynamic presentations that do not fit classic tamponade physiology.
Teaching points:

Subcostal view may appear normal; always check all windows.
Echogenic or heterogeneous fluid suggests blood, clot, or exudate.
Requires formal echo and cardiac surgery consultation — bedside pericardiocentesis is often not safe or effective.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Post-procedure hypotension
Clinical scenario: A 68-year-old man undergoes a right heart catheterization for pulmonary hypertension workup. Thirty minutes after the procedure he is hypotensive (BP 82/50), tachycardic (HR 118), and mildly diaphoretic. The team is considering IV fluids and a vasopressor.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound, subcostal view first.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Large circumferential effusion. RA free wall collapses in systole. RV diastolic collapse present on subcostal and PLAX. IVC 2.4 cm, non-collapsing.
How does this change management? Stop fluids — they will not correct tamponade. Call interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery simultaneously. Prepare for emergent pericardiocentesis. Do not start a vasopressor as the primary intervention; it temporizes without fixing the problem.



Case 2: Dyspnea in a cancer patient
Clinical scenario: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma presents with two weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea and fullness in her chest. BP 104/72, HR 102, RR 20. JVD present. CXR shows enlarged cardiac silhouette.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound — subcostal and PLAX minimum.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Very large circumferential effusion with swinging heart motion. No chamber collapse. IVC 2.2 cm with minimal respiratory variation.
How does this change management? Large effusion without tamponade physiology at this moment — but high risk. Oncology and cardiology consultation for semi-elective pericardiocentesis or pericardial window. Admit for monitoring. Do not discharge based on the absence of tamponade physiology now — large malignant effusions can decompensate rapidly.



Case 3: Undifferentiated shock in the ED
Clinical scenario: A 44-year-old man arrives by EMS after being found unresponsive. BP 70/40, HR 124, GCS 10. No history available. Cool, mottled, distended neck veins.
What exam would you perform? Immediate subcostal cardiac view as part of the resuscitation.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Moderate effusion. RA collapse in systole. No obvious RV collapse (limited image quality).
How does this change management? Activate the pericardiocentesis team. Limit IV fluids to one bolus as a bridge. Avoid deep sedation if intubation is needed — it can precipitate cardiac arrest in tamponade by eliminating sympathetic tone. If the patient arrests, perform pericardiocentesis before standard ACLS measures; defibrillation will not work if the heart cannot fill.



Case 4: Dialysis patient with chest pain
Clinical scenario: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis three times weekly presents with sharp chest pain worse lying flat. He missed his last two dialysis sessions. Vitals stable. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for effusion and tamponade physiology.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Small-to-moderate posterior effusion. No chamber collapse. IVC 2.5 cm (consistent with volume overload from missed dialysis).
How does this change management? Uremic pericarditis with a small effusion. Arrange urgent dialysis — this is the treatment. NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated in ESRD. Admit for monitoring and repeat ultrasound after dialysis. Uremic effusions can enlarge rapidly if dialysis is delayed.



Case 5: Trauma — thoracic injury
Clinical scenario: A 29-year-old woman is intubated in the field after a high-speed MVC. BP 88/60 on two vasopressors, HR 135. Bilateral breath sounds. No obvious external thoracic trauma.
What exam would you perform? FAST exam with focused cardiac view as the first priority.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Echo-free stripe anterior to the RV on subcostal view. RV diastolic collapse present. No obvious pleural effusions.
How does this change management? Hemopericardium with tamponade physiology. Emergent cardiothoracic surgery consultation. Pericardiocentesis alone is a bridge — the underlying injury requires operative repair. If the patient arrests, ED thoracotomy with pericardiotomy is indicated per ATLS protocol. Do not spend time on CT imaging.



Case 6: Recurrent chest pain after pericarditis
Clinical scenario: A 35-year-old man treated for acute pericarditis 3 months ago returns with recurrent pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fever. His prior echo showed a small effusion that resolved at 4-week follow-up.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for recurrent effusion and LV function.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Small posterior effusion. No tamponade physiology. Normal LV function.
How does this change management? Recurrent pericarditis with small effusion — no high-risk features. Restart NSAIDs and colchicine. If not already on colchicine, prescribe it now. Cardiology consultation for a second or third recurrence — consider IL-1 inhibitor therapy (anakinra, rilonacept).






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. On PLAX, you see an echo-free space posterior to the LV. How do you determine whether it is pericardial or pleural?






Caution





Answer Locate the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section at the far left of the PLAX image. Fluid anterior to the aorta is pericardial. Fluid posterior to the aorta is pleural.



Q2. A patient has a large effusion and is hypotensive. RV diastolic collapse is not clearly visible (poor image quality). What other findings support tamponade physiology?






Caution





Answer RA free wall collapse in systole (more sensitive, less specific), plethoric non-collapsing IVC (>2.1 cm, <50% inspiratory collapse), and respiratory variation on mitral inflow >25% by PW Doppler. No single finding is required — the diagnosis is integrative.



Q3. You see an echogenic structure anterior to the RV that does not move with the cardiac cycle. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how do you confirm it?






Caution





Answer Pericardial fat pad. Confirm by noting echogenicity (not anechoic), anterior location, and absence of positional shift. Reposition the patient — a true effusion will layer dependently; fat will not.



Q4. A patient with known metastatic cancer has a large effusion but no chamber collapse. Is this patient safe for discharge?






Caution





Answer No. Absence of tamponade physiology at this moment does not mean discharge is safe. Large malignant effusions can decompensate rapidly. This patient needs admission, oncology and cardiology consultation, and a plan for drainage or a pericardial window.



Q5. What are the high-risk features in acute pericarditis that warrant hospitalization?






Caution





Answer Large effusion (>2 cm), tamponade physiology, fever >38°C with subacute onset, immunocompromised state, anticoagulation therapy, failure to respond to NSAIDs within 1 week, and evidence of myocardial involvement (elevated troponin, wall motion abnormality).



Q6. In a trauma patient with tamponade physiology, why is pericardiocentesis alone often insufficient?






Caution





Answer Traumatic hemopericardium usually indicates cardiac or great vessel injury. Pericardiocentesis may temporarily relieve pressure, but the underlying structural injury requires operative repair. Definitive management is in the operating room.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is global LV systolic function normal, reduced, or hyperdynamic? A visual estimate of ejection fraction — severely reduced, mildly-to-moderately reduced, normal, or hyperdynamic — is sufficient for bedside decision-making. You do not need a number.
Are there regional wall motion abnormalities? Segmental dysfunction in a coronary distribution suggests ACS as the etiology. Global dysfunction is more consistent with cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, or sepsis-mediated depression. The distinction changes management immediately.



Bedside LV assessment answers the most fundamental question in hemodynamic resuscitation: is the pump failing? A hypotensive patient with a hyperdynamic LV does not need inotropes — they need volume, vasopressors, or treatment of the underlying distributive state. A hypotensive patient with a severely reduced EF and dilated LV is in cardiogenic shock and needs a fundamentally different approach. Getting this wrong early leads to fluid overload in cardiogenic shock or undertreated distributive shock.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. LV function is assessed across multiple windows — no single view is sufficient. The goal is to visualize the LV in two orthogonal planes and assess wall motion in all segments.


Parasternal long axis






Tip



Video slot: PLAX for LV assessment — M-mode placement at mitral valve tips, visual EF estimation, posterior wall and septal motion.



What you are looking for: Global LV contractility (do the walls move vigorously inward in systole?), chamber size (a dilated LV suggests chronicity), and mitral valve excursion (reduced in low-output states). M-mode at the tips of the mitral valve leaflets allows measurement of EPSS (E-point septal separation) — a distance greater than 7 mm suggests reduced EF.



Parasternal short axis — papillary muscle level






Tip



Video slot: PSAX at papillary muscle level — the “donut” view, eyeball EF, D-sign assessment.



What you are looking for: The LV should appear round in cross-section and contract concentrically and symmetrically. This is the best single view for a visual EF estimate — watch the endocardium sweep inward in systole. Also assess the interventricular septum: a flat or D-shaped LV indicates RV pressure or volume overload (see Module 3).



Apical four-chamber






Tip



Video slot: Apical four-chamber for wall motion — septal, lateral, apical segments.



What you are looking for: All four chambers, with attention to LV wall motion in each visible segment. The apical view is essential for identifying apical wall motion abnormalities (LAD territory) and for assessing LV size relative to the RV.



Subcostal






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal cardiac view — rapid global LV assessment in the undifferentiated patient.



When to use: First-line in the unstable patient who cannot be repositioned. Provides a rapid visual impression of global LV function. Not sufficient alone for wall motion analysis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
3. Normal & normal variants
The library of normal hearts and common confounders.






Tip



Video slots: Normal LV function across body habitus — thin patient, obese patient, patient with LVH. Review before the pathology library.




Normal LV systolic function
Normal EF is 55–70%. On visual assessment, the endocardial walls should move briskly inward in systole and the LV cavity should appear to nearly obliterate at peak contraction. The posterior wall and septum thicken in systole. A normal study looks vigorous — if you are unsure whether the function is normal, it probably is.


Hyperdynamic LV
EF greater than 70%, often with near-complete cavity obliteration in systole. Common in sepsis (early), anemia, hyperthyroidism, and hypovolemia. The hyperdynamic LV in a hypotensive patient points away from cardiogenic shock as the primary etiology — though it does not rule out mixed shock states.


LV hypertrophy
Increased wall thickness (septum or posterior wall >11 mm). Concentric hypertrophy (thick walls, normal cavity size) is seen in chronic hypertension and aortic stenosis. Eccentric hypertrophy (thick walls with a dilated cavity) suggests chronic volume overload. Hypertrophied ventricles are at higher risk for diastolic dysfunction and may decompensate with tachycardia or aggressive fluid loading.


“Kissing walls” in hypovolemia
In severe hypovolemia, the LV cavity may appear nearly obliterated even in diastole, with the walls nearly touching. This is distinct from a true reduction in EF — function appears hyperdynamic, not depressed. Seen in hemorrhagic shock, third-spacing, and aggressive diuresis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Severely reduced EF






Tip



Video slot: Severely reduced EF — dilated LV, minimal wall motion, large end-systolic volume.





EF visually estimated below 30%. The LV is often dilated. Wall motion is globally reduced with minimal inward thickening in systole. The mitral valve opens sluggishly and EPSS is markedly increased.
Teaching points:

This is cardiogenic shock physiology until proven otherwise in a hypotensive patient.
Causes: ischemic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, Takotsubo, sepsis-mediated depression (usually less severe).
Avoid aggressive fluid loading — the failing LV cannot handle preload augmentation and you will worsen pulmonary edema.
Inotropes (dobutamine) and early consideration of mechanical circulatory support are the interventions.




Mildly to moderately reduced EF






Tip



Video slot: Moderately reduced EF — reduced but present wall motion, mildly dilated LV.




EF visually estimated 30–50%. Wall motion is reduced but clearly present. The LV may or may not be dilated. This pattern is common in known heart failure with reduced EF presenting with decompensation.
Teaching points:

Does not automatically mean cardiogenic shock — assess for hemodynamic compromise and end-organ perfusion.
Treat the precipitant: arrhythmia, ischemia, infection, medication non-compliance, dietary indiscretion.
Avoid negative inotropes and large fluid boluses.




Regional wall motion abnormalities






Tip



Video slots: - Anterior RWMA (LAD territory) — apical and anterior wall hypokinesis - Inferior RWMA (RCA territory) — inferior and posterior wall hypokinesis - Lateral RWMA (LCx territory) — lateral wall hypokinesis




Segmental dysfunction confined to a coronary distribution. The affected wall moves less than adjacent segments or is akinetic (no motion) or dyskinetic (paradoxical outward motion in systole).
Teaching points:

New RWMA with hemodynamic compromise = acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Activate the cath lab.
Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present — RCA occlusion may cause concomitant RV infarct, which requires different management (avoid nitrates, volume-load to maintain RV preload).
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: apical ballooning with preserved or hyperdynamic basal segments — does not follow a coronary distribution. History of emotional or physiologic stressor.




Dilated LV






Tip



Video slot: Dilated LV — increased end-diastolic dimension, loss of the normal elliptical shape.




LV end-diastolic diameter greater than 5.5 cm (PLAX, M-mode) or a visually enlarged chamber. Dilation suggests chronicity — the heart has had time to remodel.
Teaching points:

A dilated LV with severely reduced EF is a chronic dilated cardiomyopathy. This patient likely has known disease and has decompensated.
A non-dilated LV with reduced EF suggests an acute process (myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute MI).
The distinction matters for prognosis and for anticipating how the LV will respond to treatment.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Hypotension after STEMI
Clinical scenario: A 61-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is brought to the ED. He received aspirin and heparin in the field. On arrival his BP is 78/50, HR 110, and he is cool and diaphoretic. The cath lab team is being activated.
What exam would you perform? Rapid focused cardiac ultrasound before transfer to the cath lab.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.



What you see: Severely reduced EF. Anterior and apical wall akinesis. LV not markedly dilated (acute presentation). No pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? This is cardiogenic shock from a large anterior MI. Start dobutamine at low dose as a bridge. Avoid aggressive fluid boluses. Notify the cath lab of cardiogenic shock — they may want an IABP or Impella placed at the time of PCI. Do not delay transfer for a prolonged echo.



Case 2: Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman with septic shock from a urinary source has been on norepinephrine for 18 hours. She received 4 L of crystalloid. Her BP is now 72/40 despite escalating vasopressors. Lactate is rising.
What exam would you perform? Bedside cardiac ultrasound — LV function, RV size, IVC.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.





What you see: Severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis. LV not dilated. IVC is plethoric.
How does this change management? This is sepsis-mediated cardiomyopathy with cardiogenic component to the shock. Add dobutamine. Stop or slow fluid administration. Consider PA catheter or advanced hemodynamic monitoring. Avoid further escalation of vasopressors alone — you are vasoconstricting a failing heart. Reassess in 4–6 hours; sepsis-mediated depression often recovers with treatment of the underlying infection.



Case 3: Chest pain and new ECG changes
Clinical scenario: A 49-year-old woman presents with 2 hours of substernal chest pressure and diaphoresis. ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6. She is hemodynamically stable.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for RWMA.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.



What you see: Lateral wall hypokinesis. Preserved global function. No effusion.
How does this change management? Lateral RWMA in the context of ST depression and chest pain is an NSTEMI with high-risk features. Activate the cath lab urgently. Anticoagulate. The echo finding corroborates the clinical diagnosis and raises urgency — do not wait for troponin results.



Case 4: Young patient with viral prodrome and shock
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old man presents with 5 days of viral URI symptoms followed by 24 hours of progressive dyspnea and now hypotension (BP 88/60). He has no cardiac history.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.



What you see: Severely reduced EF. Globally hypokinetic but not dilated LV. No RWMA pattern. Small pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Myocarditis with cardiogenic shock. This is not ischemic cardiomyopathy — no regional pattern, young patient, viral prodrome. Avoid NSAIDs (may worsen myocarditis). Start dobutamine. Urgent cardiology consultation for consideration of mechanical circulatory support — myocarditis-related shock can be rapidly fatal and some patients benefit from short-term MCS as a bridge to recovery. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis but should not delay resuscitation.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. A hypotensive patient has a hyperdynamic LV on bedside echo. What does this tell you about the etiology of shock?






Caution





Answer Hyperdynamic LV function argues against cardiogenic shock as the primary etiology. Consider distributive shock (sepsis, anaphylaxis), hypovolemia, or obstructive shock. Mixed shock states are possible — a hyperdynamic LV does not guarantee adequate cardiac output if heart rate is severely elevated.



Q2. What is EPSS, and what does an elevated value indicate?






Caution





Answer E-point septal separation — the distance between the anterior mitral leaflet at its maximum opening excursion (E-point) and the interventricular septum, measured by M-mode on PLAX. Normal is less than 7 mm. Values above 7 mm correlate with reduced EF. It is a useful single-number surrogate when visual estimation is uncertain.



Q3. You see hypokinesis of the inferior wall and posterior wall on PSAX. What coronary territory does this implicate, and what additional structure should you assess?






Caution





Answer Right coronary artery (RCA) territory. Always assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present — the RCA supplies the RV free wall and an RCA occlusion can cause concomitant RV infarct. RV infarct requires volume loading and avoidance of nitrates, making it a distinct management scenario.



Q4. A patient has a severely reduced EF with a markedly dilated LV. A second patient has a severely reduced EF with a normal-sized LV. What does the difference in LV size suggest?






Caution





Answer Dilation suggests a chronic process — the heart has had time to remodel (dilated cardiomyopathy, longstanding ischemic disease). A non-dilated LV with severely reduced EF suggests an acute process: myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute large MI, or acute decompensation of previously compensated disease.



Q5. What is the Takotsubo pattern, and how does it differ from an LAD occlusion on bedside echo?






Caution





Answer Takotsubo (apical ballooning syndrome) shows apical and mid-ventricular hypokinesis or akinesis with preserved or hyperdynamic basal segments. An LAD occlusion causes anterior and apical dysfunction but typically includes some basal anterior involvement and follows the LAD distribution more closely. Takotsubo does not respect a single coronary territory — the basal sparing is the key distinguishing feature.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
Bedside cardiac ultrasound begins with four standard windows. Each window shows the heart from a different acoustic angle, and each reveals structures that the others cannot. No single window is sufficient for a complete exam — the goal is to build a three-dimensional mental model of the heart by integrating what you see across all four views.
This module covers:

Machine setup and probe selection
How to obtain each window reliably
The normal anatomy visible in each view
Common normal variants

Pathology is introduced in later modules. The goal here is to recognize a normal study confidently before encountering abnormalities.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
1. Machine setup
Probe: Phased array (cardiac) probe. The small footprint fits between ribs; the sector beam provides the wide near-field needed to visualize the full heart. A curvilinear probe is an acceptable substitute when a phased array is unavailable. A linear probe is not appropriate for cardiac imaging.
Preset: Select the cardiac preset. This does two important things:

Inverts the depth convention so the apex appears at the top of the screen in apical views (cardiac orientation).
Optimizes gain, frequency, and frame rate for cardiac imaging.

Depth: Adjust so the far wall of the structure of interest is visible with a small margin beyond it. Too little depth clips posterior structures; too much depth makes cardiac structures appear small and reduces resolution.
Gain: Adjust so that blood appears dark (anechoic) and myocardium appears mid-gray. An overgained image obscures the distinction between fluid and tissue.
Indicator convention: In cardiac imaging, the probe indicator is displayed on the right side of the screen. Confirm this on your machine before starting — some machines default to the left (radiology convention). If the indicator is on the wrong side, the image will be mirrored.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
2. The four standard windows


Subcostal four-chamber view






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal four-chamber acquisition — probe position, indicator orientation, fanning technique, optimization tips.






Subcostal four-chamber probe placement. The probe sits subxiphoid, nearly flat against the abdomen. The red indicator dot points to the patient’s left.


Probe placement: Subxiphoid, probe nearly flat against the abdomen (15–20° angle above horizontal). Indicator points to the patient’s left. Use the left lobe of the liver as an acoustic window.
How to optimize:

Ask the patient to inhale slowly and hold — this drops the diaphragm and brings the heart into the imaging plane.
Apply firm, steady pressure. Sustained pressure displaces bowel gas and improves the window.
If the view is poor, move the probe slightly to the right (more liver), or ask the patient to bend their knees to relax the abdominal wall.
In intubated or supine patients, this is often the most accessible window and does not require repositioning.

Why this window first: In undifferentiated shock or cardiac arrest, the subcostal view is the fastest to obtain and does not require repositioning the patient. It is the window most likely to be achievable in a supine, ventilated patient.



Parasternal long axis






Tip



Video slot: Parasternal long axis acquisition — rib interspace selection, indicator toward the right shoulder, tilting to optimize the LV long axis.






Parasternal long axis probe placement. Left parasternal border, 3rd–4th ICS. The red indicator dot points toward the patient’s right shoulder (~10–11 o’clock).


Probe placement: Left parasternal border, 3rd or 4th intercostal space, indicator pointing toward the patient’s right shoulder (approximately 10–11 o’clock). The imaging plane cuts through the long axis of the left ventricle.
How to optimize:

Move up or down one rib space if the LV appears foreshortened or the apex is cut off.
Tilt the probe slightly medially or laterally to bring the aortic root and LV into the same plane.
The aortic valve should appear central and open symmetrically in systole.
The LV walls should appear equal in thickness and the chamber should not appear foreshortened.

Parasternal short axis probe placement. Starting from PLAX, rotate 90° clockwise. The indicator moves to the patient’s left shoulder (~1–2 o’clock). The ghost probe (faint) shows the PLAX starting position.


Probe placement: Same position as PLAX, then rotate the probe 90° clockwise — indicator moves toward the patient’s left shoulder (approximately 1–2 o’clock). The imaging plane now cuts the heart in cross-section.
Fanning between levels: Tilt the probe toward the right shoulder (base) to image higher cross-sections; tilt toward the left hip (apex) to image lower cross-sections.
How to optimize:

At the papillary muscle level, the LV should appear round, not oval. An oval appearance means the plane is slightly oblique — adjust.
At the aortic valve level, all three cusps should be visible on closure.

Probe placement: Point of maximal impulse (PMI), typically 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. Indicator points toward the patient’s left and slightly inferior (4–5 o’clock) — i.e., toward the left hip, not straight lateral. This inferolateral rotation aligns the imaging plane through the long axis of the LV from apex to base and is the orientation specified by ASE guidelines. A pure 3 o’clock orientation tends to foreshorten the apex. The imaging plane shows all four chambers simultaneously.

Left lateral decubitus positioning brings the heart toward the chest wall and significantly improves image quality — use it whenever possible.
In the cardiac preset, the apex should appear at the top of the screen. Reduce depth so the apex sits at the top with a small margin.

Right AV valve — inserts slightly more apically than mitral


Left atrium
Bottom left


Right atrium
Bottom right


Interventricular septum
Vertical, separates LV and RV


Interatrial septum
Thin membrane between LA and RA



Key observation: The tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically on the interventricular septum than the mitral valve. This normal apical offset reliably identifies which AV valve is which when orientation is uncertain.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. You place the probe at the left parasternal border with the indicator pointing toward the right shoulder. Which window are you in? Name four structures you expect to see.






Caution





Answer Parasternal long axis (PLAX). Expected structures include: right ventricle (near-field), interventricular septum, left ventricle, anterior and posterior mitral valve leaflets, left atrium, aortic valve, aortic root/LVOT, and the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section at the far left.



Q2. You are in PLAX and want to move to PSAX. What do you do with the probe?






Caution





Answer Rotate the probe 90° clockwise from the PLAX position. The indicator moves from pointing toward the right shoulder to pointing toward the left shoulder (approximately 1–2 o’clock). The imaging plane now cuts the heart in cross-section.



Q3. In the subcostal four-chamber view, which cardiac chamber is closest to the probe? What structure serves as the acoustic window?






Caution





Answer The right ventricle is closest to the probe. The left lobe of the liver serves as the acoustic window.



Q4. On PSAX at the aortic valve level, you see three cusps forming a Y-shape on closure. What is this called, and what does it confirm?






Caution





Answer The Mercedes-Benz sign. It confirms a normal tricuspid aortic valve with three cusps — right coronary, left coronary, and non-coronary. If only two cusps are visible with an oval “fish mouth” opening, consider a bicuspid aortic valve.



Q5. In the apical four-chamber view, how do you distinguish the mitral valve from the tricuspid valve?






Caution





Answer The tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically on the interventricular septum than the mitral valve — this apical offset is the key distinguishing feature. The tricuspid is on the right side of the image (associated with the RV and RA); the mitral is on the left (associated with the LV and LA).



Q6. At the papillary muscle level on PSAX, you see two echogenic nodular structures on the LV wall. What are they, and where are they located?






Caution





Answer The anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles. The anterolateral papillary muscle is on the lateral wall; the posteromedial papillary muscle is on the inferior wall. They are the attachment points for the chordae tendineae that tether the mitral valve leaflets.



Q7. You see a thin, linear echogenic structure crossing the LV cavity from wall to wall on apical four-chamber. It does not move independently. What is it, and is it pathologic?






Caution





Answer A false tendon (aberrant chordae tendineae). This is a normal variant — a fixed, linear structure without hemodynamic significance. It should not be mistaken for a vegetation (which is irregular and attached to a valve leaflet) or intracardiac thrombus (which is typically at the apex and has a different morphology).

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is the RV dilated or failing? A visually enlarged RV — approaching or exceeding the size of the LV — is the primary finding. Normal RV is roughly two-thirds the size of the LV on apical four-chamber view.
What is the cause, and does it require immediate intervention? RV failure from massive PE is a needle/catheter emergency. RV failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension or ARDS needs a different approach. The echo does not always give you the diagnosis — it gives you the hemodynamic phenotype to guide management.



The RV is the chamber most often underappreciated in critical care. It operates as a low-pressure, high-compliance structure that tolerates volume overload relatively well but is exquisitely sensitive to acute pressure increases. When RV afterload rises acutely — as in massive PE — the RV dilates rapidly, shifts the interventricular septum, impairs LV filling, and drives the patient into obstructive shock. Recognizing this pattern quickly and accurately is one of the highest-yield skills in critical care echo.
